Netflix’s war drama ‘Operation Safed Sagar’ has earned attention for its portrayal of the
Indian Air Force’s role during the
Kargil War, but filming the series proved to be a demanding experience for its cast and crew.
Abhay Verma, who plays Flying Officer Rajpal Singh Dhaliwal aka Dhali, has now recalled shooting in extreme weather conditions, travelling to high-altitude locations and getting the rare opportunity to sit inside a MiG-21.
Abhay Verma on seeing India like never before
Opening up about his experience on The Great Indian Kapil Show, working on Operation Safed Sagar, actor Abhay Verma, who plays Flying Officer Rajpal Singh Dhaliwal a.k.a. Dhali in the show, admitted that the job gave him the opportunity to see facets of India he had never witnessed before. "What I saw while shooting for the show, I had never seen anything like it before. I didn't know our country was so beautiful. This was the first time I saw snow. I also experienced extreme heat for the first time," he shared.
He went on to describe the physical toll of the shoot: "We shot in Bikaner, Rajasthan, and it gets extremely hot there. We filmed at an Air Force base. So, I experienced extreme heat and cold, saw snowfall, and also saw people fall (faint). It was a very different experience. Since we didn't have our phones with us, those memories still live with us. It was a golden time; had we had our phones with us, the journey wouldn't have been as memorable," Abhay added.
Abhay Verma's emotional wrap
Abhay also admitted feeling sad when filming wrapped, reflecting on just how singular the experience was. "That world was so different. But all of us can proudly say that we were the last ones to sit in a MiG-21 (Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21, a supersonic jet fighter and interceptor aircraft)."
Why Jimmy Shergill's makeup artist quit
Revealing that the team had to commute for over two hours to reach certain sets located atop mountains, actor Jimmy Shergill, who plays Wing Commander BS 'Tony' Dhanoa, shared that at one point his makeup artist quit because he could no longer withstand the weather.
"We shot in the mountains at altitudes of 16,000-17,000 feet. It took us two to two and a half hours to drive to where our set was located. One day, my makeup artist came to my vanity van, saying, 'I have had enough! Enough with all the respect, I am leaving! Stop me if you can.' Now, you can imagine how exhausted that man must have been. He had been with me for 30 years, since Maachis (1996). And he left, just like that," Shergill shared.
Arnav Bhasin calls it his 'biggest project' yet
Arnav Bhasin, who plays Flying Officer Amit Gupta a.k.a. Goofy in Operation Safed Sagar, called the Netflix series his "biggest project" to date. "I learned so much from it. Everyone here taught me so wholeheartedly. Every question that I had, they answered. I knew nothing about Operation Safed Sagar because I was just born during the war (Kargil War). I am just 27 now, and that's pretty much how long it's been since Operation Safed Sagar. So, through this show, I learned a lot," he noted.
About 'Operation Safed Sagar'
Directed by Oni Sen, 'Operation Safed Sagar' is a Netflix series that chronicles the Indian Air Force's role during the 1999 Kargil War, drawing its name from the real-life military operation. The show stars Jimmy Shergill as Wing Commander BS 'Tony' Dhanoa, alongside Abhay Verma and Arnav Bhasin in key roles, and has received widely favourable reviews for its gripping recreation of the aerial campaign. Shot extensively at real Air Force bases and in extreme mountain terrain, the series has struck a chord with audiences for its authenticity and its tribute to the pilots who served during the conflict.

Britain could be gripped by a sixth heatwave next month, according to the Met Office.
The fifth heatwave of the summer peaked last Thursday with temperatures reaching their hottest of the year at 38.1C in Kew Gardens, London.
During last week’s heatwave, two trains derailed in the South East, the first in Lewes, East Sussex, on Thursday, seriously injuring two. A second came off the tracks at Wickford in Essex less than 24 hours later.
Network Rail chiefs have said the heat may have been to blame, and investigations are under way.
The stretch of line between Haywards Heath and Lewes where the first train derailed would remain closed for 10 more days, Network Rail said.
It said: “Customers travelling next week, and in the weeks ahead, are advised to check before they travel and, where possible, use alternative train services via Brighton.
“Rail replacement buses will run between Lewes and Haywards Heath, serving Cooksbridge and Plumpton. These buses have limited capacity, so customers travelling to other stations should travel via Brighton instead.”
Network Rail said tickets would be accepted on alternative Southern, Thameslink and Southeastern services as well as Brighton and Hove buses and London Underground services between London terminal stations.
Britain has endured the driest July since records began in 1836, and the whole of Wales and nearly three-quarters of England are officially in drought. There are widespread hosepipe bans across southern England.
High temperatures and unprecedented drought have led to wildfires, with as many so far this year in England and Wales – 1,017 – as in all of last year, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council. The 2025 tally was the highest ever recorded.
The fires caused devastation in Stourbridge, West Midlands, where 19 homes were destroyed, while 100 military personnel were deployed across South Wales to fight blazes there.
They prompted the Government’s “most extensive use” yet of Britain’s emergency alert system, which warned that wildfires could be caused by barbecues and fireworks.
However, the decision to use the system was criticised by some as unnecessary.
Dudley Borough Council said in an update on Sunday that eight families whose houses had been destroyed by the fires had been able to view their properties.
Some 13 households whose properties had been partially damaged in the blazes had been able to return, chief executive Balvinder Heran said in a residents’ briefing.
Last week, the Met Office said Britain was on track to endure its hottest recorded summer, surpassing that of 1976, when the average daily maximum temperature was 21C.
This summer’s heat has passed milestones including the most days recorded above 30C and 36C and hottest-day records for May and June.
The NHS said the heat had meant A&E wards had had their busiest summer ever, with a record 2.5 million patients in July.
Summer usually results in an increase in demand because of a rise in accidents from people spending more time outdoors.
This year it has been exacerbated by the hot and dry weather, with more people suffering from dehydration, breathing issues, and the worsening of underlying medical conditions.
Nurses have warned that they are caring for patients in conditions “not fit for humans” because of a lack of air conditioning and ventilation.
Yvette Cooper, the Health Secretary, has pledged that the NHS will start preparing for summer in the same way it does for winter.

DH reminds public to take precautions against heat-related illnesses during very hot weather
The Centre for Health Protection (CHP) of the Department of Health (DH) today (August 17) reminded members of the public to take appropriate precautions against heat-related illnesses, such as heat cramps, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, during very hot weather.
In a high-temperature environment, excessive sweating and difficulty in heat dissipation can cause stress to the body. Members of the public should take the following precautions:
- Hydrate in a timely manner to prevent dehydration;
- Wear light-coloured, loose-fitting and breathable clothing to minimise heat absorption and facilitate perspiration and heat dissipation;
- Keep indoor areas well ventilated and maintain appropriate temperature and humidity, e.g. by opening windows or using a fan or air-conditioning;
- Avoid strenuous exercise and prolonged activities such as hiking or trekking;
- Arrange outdoor activities in the morning or the late afternoon, if possible, and bring enough water; and
- Avoid beverages containing caffeine, such as coffee and tea, as well as alcoholic beverages, which may speed up water loss through the urinary system.
In addition, infants and children, the elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses such as heart disease or high blood pressure, overweight people and outdoor/manual workers are more susceptible to heat stroke. These groups should pay special attention to the following:
- Infants and young children: Avoid going outside when the temperature is high. If they must go outside, adults should ensure they stay in places with moderate temperatures and good ventilation or air-conditioning. Infants and young children should never be left unattended in a confined space such as a vehicle;
- The elderly, pregnant women, individuals with chronic illnesses and overweight people: Pay close attention to health conditions and seek help as soon as possible if experiencing any abnormalities in health indicators such as blood pressure, heart rate, etc or if there are fluctuations in health conditions. Avoid going out when the temperature is high. Make sure there is good ventilation, or turn on a fan or air-conditioner to keep an appropriate temperature indoors. High temperatures can also worsen the condition of people with chronic illnesses (such as cardiovascular and respiratory diseases). Therefore, they should have an ample supply of their usual medication and keep in contact with family members, neighbours and the community. People should seek immediate help if they feel unwell.
- Outdoor/manual workers: Reschedule work to cooler hours as far as feasible. If working in a hot environment is unavoidable, provide shade where practicable and use ventilation and heat dissipation equipment. Once work has begun, gradually adjust the pace of work and take breaks in the shade to regain strength.
The DH reminded the public that heat stroke is one of the most common health risks in hot weather. Over the past five years, there have been over 200 hospital admissions due to heat stroke each year in Hong Kong, with two to five fatal cases occurring mainly during the summer months from May to September. Vulnerable groups are more susceptible to heat stroke. Symptoms include dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion. In severe cases, patients may suffer from convulsions or become unconscious, which can be life-threatening if they are not cooled down and resuscitated in a timely manner.
Members of the public are also advised to pay attention to the latest weather, as well as the real-time and forecasted ultraviolet (UV) index released by the Hong Kong Observatory (HKO). When the UV index is high (6 or above), the public should note the following:
- Avoid direct sunlight exposure to the skin and the eyes;
- Apply broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen liberally, with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 30 or higher, when participating in outdoor activities. Reapply every two hours if staying outdoors for long periods, or after swimming, sweating or towelling off;
- While using DEET-containing insect repellents for personal protection against mosquito-borne diseases, apply sunscreen before insect repellent;
If symptoms develop, such as dizziness, headache, nausea, shortness of breath or confusion, rest and seek help immediately, and seek medical advice as soon as possible.
